title: How Computers Learn: Artificial Intelligence
summary: How computers learn patterns from labeled data, how AI helps people every day, and why its mistakes and bias mean humans must check its work.
poll: Artificial intelligence does more good than harm.

versions.title: Can a Computer Learn?
versions.text:
You talk to a phone. It types what you say. How? It learned!

A computer does what it is told. The list of steps is a program. People write it.

Some jobs have too many rules. Look at a cat and a dog. You know which is which. But it is hard to write all the rules.

So people train it. They give it data. Data is lots of facts and pics. It sees lots of cat pics. Each one says "cat." It looks for a pattern. That is a thing you see again and again.

Then it makes a guess. Is this a cat? If it is wrong, it fixes its math. It tries once more. Bit by bit, it gets good. We call this AI.

AI helps us. It can change words to a new tongue. It can tell which roads are full. It helps doctors look at scans.

But AI can make a mistake. It learns from its data. Bad data can teach it wrong things. So we must check its work.

Saudi Arabia has a big team for AI. Kids there learn to code, too.

Then the computer makes a guess. Is this new picture a cat? If it is wrong, it changes its math a bit and tries again. Little by little, it gets better. This is called AI, or artificial intelligence.

versions.title: How Computers Learn
versions.text:
You speak to a phone, and it types your words. A map app shows you the fastest road home. How do they do it? The computer learned how!

A computer does exactly what it is told. The list of steps it follows is called a program. People write programs carefully, one step at a time.

However, some jobs have too many rules to write. Think about a cat and a dog. You can tell them apart in a second. Still, it is very hard to write down every rule that explains how you know.

So people train the computer instead. They give it data, which is a large set of facts, numbers, or pictures. For example, they might show it thousands of photos of cats. Each photo is marked "cat." The computer searches for a pattern, something that shows up again and again, like pointed ears or whiskers.

Next, the computer makes a guess about a new photo. If its guess is wrong, it changes its math a little and tries again. Little by little, it gets better. When a computer learns like this, we call it AI, or artificial intelligence.

AI helps people in many ways. It can translate words from one language to another. It can tell which roads are crowded. It can even help doctors study scans of the body.

But AI can still make a mistake. It only knows what its data teaches it. If the data is wrong or unfair, the computer learns wrong things. That is why people must always check its work.

Saudi Arabia has a national group that leads its work on AI. Many students are learning to code, too.

versions.title: How Computers Learn: Artificial Intelligence
versions.text:
You speak to a phone, and it types your words. A map app warns you about traffic before you leave home. How can a machine do these things? The answer is that the computer has learned.

A computer does exactly what it is told. The set of steps it follows is called a program, and a step-by-step plan for solving a problem is called an algorithm. For many jobs, people write every rule themselves.

However, some jobs have too many rules to write. You can recognize a cat in a second, but try to explain every rule for how you know. It is almost impossible!

So people train the computer instead. They give it data, a large set of facts, numbers, or pictures. For example, they might show it thousands of photos, each with a label that says "cat" or "not cat." The computer searches for a pattern, such as pointed ears or whiskers, that shows up again and again.

Next, the computer makes a guess about a new photo. If the guess is wrong, it adjusts its math a little and tries again. After many tries, it becomes quite accurate. When a computer learns this way, we call it artificial intelligence, or AI.

AI helps people every day. It can translate words from one language to another. It can predict which roads will be crowded. It can even help doctors find signs of illness in scans of the body.

Still, AI can make a mistake. It only knows what its data teaches it, so if the data is wrong or unfair, the computer learns wrong things. That is why people must check its work.

In Saudi Arabia, a national authority leads the country's work on AI, and many students are learning to code.

versions.title: Teaching Machines to Think: Artificial Intelligence
versions.text:
You speak to a phone, and it types your words almost perfectly. A map application warns you about traffic before you even leave home. These machines seem clever, but their skill comes from a process in which the computer has learned from experience.

Traditionally, a computer does precisely what it is instructed to do. The instructions it follows form a program, and a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem is called an algorithm. For many tasks, programmers write every rule themselves.

However, some tasks involve far too many rules to write. You can recognize a cat instantly, yet explaining every rule your brain uses to decide is nearly impossible.

Consequently, engineers use a method called machine learning. Rather than writing the rules, they provide the computer with data, an enormous collection of examples. They might show it thousands of photographs, each with a label that says "cat" or "not cat," and the computer searches for patterns, such as pointed ears or whiskers, that appear again and again. Many of these systems use a neural network, which is a structure of connected layers loosely inspired by the way cells in the brain link together.

The computer then makes a prediction about an unfamiliar photograph. If the prediction is incorrect, it adjusts its internal calculations slightly and tries again. After thousands of attempts, it becomes remarkably accurate, and when a computer performs tasks that normally require human thinking, we call it artificial intelligence, or AI.

AI assists people every day. It translates sentences between languages, predicts which roads will become congested, and helps doctors identify early signs of illness in medical scans.

Nevertheless, AI has important limits. It understands only what its data teaches it, so if the examples are inaccurate or incomplete, the system can develop a bias, an unfair tendency to favor some answers or groups over others. It also does not truly understand the world or feel anything the way people do. For these reasons, building AI raises ethical questions about fairness, privacy, and responsibility, and humans must always check its work.

In Saudi Arabia, a national authority for data and AI, established in 2019, guides the country's plans, and many students are learning to write computer code.

versions.title: Teaching Machines to Think: Artificial Intelligence
versions.text:
When a smartphone transcribes spoken words with near-flawless accuracy, or a navigation application anticipates traffic congestion before a journey has even commenced, these technological systems appear remarkably, even unsettlingly, intelligent; however, their operational capabilities originate not from an exhaustive catalog of explicitly programmed rules but from a sophisticated process through which the computational system has genuinely learned from accumulated empirical experience rather than predetermined instruction.

Conventionally, a computer executes precisely and exclusively what it has been explicitly instructed to perform, with such sequential instructions collectively constituting what is termed a program, while a systematic, sequential procedure specifically designed to resolve a particular computational problem is termed an algorithm; consequently, for numerous conventional tasks, programmers must compose every governing rule themselves, explicitly, exhaustively, and without exception.

However, certain cognitively complex tasks involve such an overwhelming multiplicity of conceivable rules that explicit articulation becomes practically unfeasible, since the instantaneous human recognition of a cat, for instance, relies upon intuitive cognitive processes so deeply ingrained that explicitly enumerating every underlying neurological rule the brain employs in reaching that determination proves practically impossible for any human to accomplish.

Consequently, engineers increasingly rely upon a computational methodology termed machine learning. Rather than manually composing explicit rules, they supply the computational system with extensive, often massive, quantities of data, vast collections of individually labeled examples, such as many thousands of photographs each explicitly designated as either "cat" or "not cat." The computational system subsequently identifies recurring statistical patterns, such as pointed ears or whiskers, that consistently characterize the target category across numerous examples. Numerous such computational systems employ what is termed a neural network, an architectural structure comprising multiple interconnected computational layers loosely, and only metaphorically, inspired by the communicative processes occurring between biological neurons within the brain.

The computational system subsequently generates probabilistic predictions regarding entirely unfamiliar photographs, and whenever a given prediction proves demonstrably incorrect, the system incrementally adjusts its internal mathematical calculations and attempts the classification anew. Following many thousands of iterative attempts and corresponding adjustments, remarkable predictive accuracy gradually emerges, and whenever a computational system performs tasks ordinarily requiring sophisticated human cognitive reasoning, this emergent capability is formally designated artificial intelligence, or AI.

AI systems assist human populations continuously throughout daily existence, translating sentences between linguistically disparate languages, anticipating with considerable accuracy which roadways will become congested, and assisting medical physicians in identifying subtle early indications of pathology within diagnostic medical imaging.

Nevertheless, artificial intelligence possesses significant, demonstrable inherent limitations that warrant careful consideration. Such systems comprehend exclusively what their underlying training data has taught them, meaning that inaccurate, incomplete, or unrepresentative examples can precipitate systematic bias, an unfair, statistically embedded tendency to favor particular outcomes or demographic groups disproportionately over others. Furthermore, artificial intelligence does not genuinely comprehend the surrounding world or experience subjective emotions in any manner analogous to authentic human experience. For these compelling and multifaceted reasons, the ongoing development of AI technology raises substantive ethical questions concerning fairness, privacy, and institutional accountability, necessitating continuous, rigorous human evaluation and oversight of its algorithmically generated decisions.

Within Saudi Arabia, a national regulatory authority dedicated specifically to data and artificial intelligence, formally established in 2019, coordinates the kingdom's comprehensive strategic approach to this rapidly evolving technological domain, while increasing numbers of students across the educational system actively pursue computer programming education in anticipation of its continued importance.

wrong.C: Roads are a different use of AI.

options: Cooking dinner for a family at home every night
Predicting which roads will be crowded
Painting houses
Planting trees
questions.why: The article says AI can predict which roads will be crowded.

wrong.A: Cooking is not mentioned.
wrong.C: Painting is not mentioned.
wrong.D: Planting trees is not mentioned.

questions.stem: What happens after the computer makes a wrong guess about a new photo?
options: It adjusts its math and tries again.
It gives up and shuts down.
It asks people to write every rule.
It throws away all the labels.
questions.why: The article says the computer adjusts its math a little and tries again, becoming more accurate over many tries.

wrong.B: The computer keeps trying.
wrong.C: The point of training is that people do not write every rule.
wrong.D: The labels are needed for learning.

questions.stem: Why does the author say it is almost impossible to explain every rule for recognizing a cat?
options: To show why training with examples is needed
To prove that cats are dangerous to small children
To say that people are not smart enough to see cats
To explain how maps work for ships at sea
questions.why: The author uses this idea to show why people train computers with examples instead of writing rules.

wrong.B: The article never says cats are dangerous.
wrong.C: The point is about rules, not intelligence.
wrong.D: Maps are discussed elsewhere.

questions.stem: Suppose a computer was trained only on photos of white cats. What might happen?
options: It would recognize every cat perfectly, whatever its color.
It might fail to recognize a black cat.
It would learn to translate languages.
It would stop needing data.
questions.why: The article says a computer only knows what its data teaches it, so missing examples could lead to wrong answers.

wrong.A: Its data would be missing many kinds of cats.
wrong.C: Cat photos do not teach translation.
wrong.D: AI always depends on its data.

questions.stem: Why must people always check the work of AI?
options: AI refuses to finish tasks that people give it, because it gets tired
AI cannot store pictures or any other files in its memory
AI only works in Saudi Arabia and nowhere else in the world
AI can learn wrong things if its data is wrong or unfair.
questions.why: The article says that if data is wrong or unfair, the computer learns wrong things, so people need to check it.

wrong.A: The article does not say AI refuses tasks.
wrong.B: AI uses thousands of pictures, so it can store them.
wrong.C: AI is used in many places.

MID.prompt: Explain why people must check the work of AI. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I used at least two details from the article.
I explained how the details support my reason.
MID.modelAnswer: People must check the work of AI because a computer only knows what its data teaches it, so if the data is wrong or unfair, the computer learns the wrong things. Even though AI can translate languages and predict which roads will be crowded, it can still recognize a pattern incorrectly and make a mistake. Checking its work makes sure the answers it gives are accurate before people trust them.

keyWords.definition: the ability of a computer to do tasks that usually need human thinking
keyWords.example: The app uses artificial intelligence to suggest the next word I want to type.

keyWords.definition: a way of building computer systems that learn from examples instead of following only written rules
keyWords.example: Engineers used machine learning so the program could sort thousands of emails.

keyWords.definition: a computer system made of connected layers that is loosely based on how brain cells link together
keyWords.example: The neural network slowly improved at reading handwritten numbers.

keyWords.definition: an unfair leaning toward some answers or groups over others
keyWords.example: The judges tried to avoid bias by hiding the names on the entries.

keyWords.definition: having to do with what is right and fair
keyWords.example: Doctors must make ethical choices to protect their patients.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Machine learning lets computers learn patterns from data, which makes AI useful but also raises limits and ethical concerns.
Neural networks are copies of the human brain, and they think exactly as people do, say the writers of the article.
Programmers no longer write algorithms, since machines do all of that work by themselves, without any help from people.
AI understands the world better than people do, and so it has no limits and no ethical concerns at all, the article says.
questions.why: The article explains machine learning, its everyday uses, and its limits such as bias and the need for human checking.

wrong.B: The article says neural networks are only loosely inspired by the brain.
wrong.C: The article says programmers still write rules for many tasks.
wrong.D: The article says AI does not truly understand the world.

questions.stem: How is machine learning different from traditional programming?
options: It uses no computers at all, because people sort every one of the photographs by hand.
It never makes predictions.
It works only with sounds.
The computer finds patterns in examples instead of following only rules people wrote.
questions.why: Traditionally, programmers write every rule; in machine learning, the computer learns patterns from labeled data.

wrong.A: Machine learning runs on computers.
wrong.B: Making predictions is a key step in machine learning.
wrong.C: The main example uses photographs.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is a neural network?
options: A group of doctors and scientists who meet to study how the human brain works
A list of labeled photographs
A structure of connected layers loosely inspired by brain cells
A national authority for data
questions.why: The article describes a neural network as connected layers loosely inspired by the way brain cells communicate.

wrong.A: It is a computer structure, not a group of people.
wrong.B: Labeled photos are the data, not the network.
wrong.D: That is the Saudi organization mentioned at the end.

questions.stem: The article says a system can develop a bias. What does bias mean in this context?
options: A strong electric current
An unfair tendency to favor some answers or groups
A very fast calculation done by thousands of connected computers
A type of medical scan
questions.why: The article defines bias as an unfair tendency to favor certain answers or groups over others.

wrong.A: Bias is not about electricity.
wrong.C: Bias is about fairness, not speed.
wrong.D: Medical scans are a separate use of AI.

questions.stem: According to the article, what can cause an AI system to develop bias?
options: Using too many computers
Learning from examples that are inaccurate or incomplete
Being turned off at night
Translating too many languages at the same time, which overloads the system
questions.why: The article says that if the examples are inaccurate or incomplete, the system can develop a bias.

wrong.A: The number of computers is not mentioned as a cause.
wrong.C: Turning off the computer is not mentioned.
wrong.D: Translation is a use, not a cause of bias.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the claim that AI does not think exactly like a person?
options: It translates sentences between languages.
It becomes remarkably accurate after thousands and thousands of practice attempts.
It does not genuinely understand the world or feel emotions.
It uses data about traffic.
questions.why: The article states that AI does not truly understand the world or feel things the way people do.

wrong.A: Translation shows a skill, not a difference from humans.
wrong.B: Accuracy shows improvement, not a difference in thinking.
wrong.D: Traffic data is just one kind of input.

questions.stem: A hospital wants to use AI to help read medical scans. Based on the article, what would be the wisest plan?
options: Let the AI decide alone, since it is always accurate and never makes a mistake in a scan.
Avoid giving the AI any examples of scans, so it learns on its own from nothing.
Use the AI, but have doctors check its results and make sure its training data is complete.
Use only one scan to train it, since one picture is enough for the AI to learn.
questions.why: The article says AI can make mistakes and develop bias, so humans must evaluate its work and its data must be complete.

wrong.A: The article says AI can be wrong and needs checking.
wrong.B: AI cannot learn without examples.
wrong.D: Learning needs thousands of examples, not one.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the paragraph about limits and ethical questions?
options: To give a balanced view by showing that AI has risks as well as benefits
To persuade readers never to use AI in their homes or at school again
To explain how to write computer code for a game on a screen
To describe the history of phones and how they changed the world
questions.why: After describing AI's uses, the author balances the article by explaining its limits and the need for fairness and human checking.

wrong.B: The author describes many helpful uses, so the goal is not to reject AI.
wrong.C: The paragraph does not teach coding.
wrong.D: Phone history is not discussed.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say AI should be allowed to make important decisions on its own. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that artificial intelligence should be allowed to make important decisions on its own. Machine learning only knows what its training data teaches it, so if that data contains bias or unfair patterns, the resulting decisions could be wrong in ways nobody notices right away. The article explains that AI can make mistakes when its data is flawed, which is exactly why people must always check its work, an ethical responsibility that disappears if a computer is left to decide alone. Because AI is a powerful tool but not a perfect judge, people should stay in charge of important decisions.

LOW.stem: What can AI do with words, according to the text?
options: Make them very loud
Hide them from people
Turn them into pictures
Put them in a new language
LOW.why: The text says AI can change words from one language to another.

wrong.A: The text does not say AI makes words loud.
wrong.B: The text does not say AI hides words.
wrong.C: The text does not say AI turns words into pictures.

LOW.stem: What can AI tell you about roads?
options: Which roads are new
Which roads are very long
Which roads are full
Which roads are wet
LOW.why: The text says AI can tell which roads are full.

wrong.A: New roads are not mentioned.
wrong.B: Road length is not mentioned.
wrong.D: Wet roads are not mentioned.

LOW.stem: AI helps doctors look at scans. What does this tell you about AI?
options: It can help with big jobs
It does all the doctors' work
It is only used for games
It never makes mistakes
LOW.why: Helping doctors shows AI can be useful for important jobs, but it still helps rather than replaces them.

wrong.B: The text says AI helps, and people must check its work.
wrong.C: The text lists several real jobs for AI.
wrong.D: The text says AI can make a mistake.

LOW.stem: Why does the author end by talking about Saudi Arabia and kids who learn to code?
options: To teach how to code well
To say AI is only for adults
To show AI matters at home
To warn that AI is very bad
LOW.why: The ending shows that Saudi Arabia has a big AI team and that kids there learn to code.

wrong.A: The article does not teach coding.
wrong.B: The text says kids learn to code too.
wrong.D: The author says AI helps us.

MID.stem: Which is an example of a pattern a computer might find in cat photos?
options: A blue sky
Pointed ears
A red ball
Green grass
MID.why: The article says the computer looks for a pattern such as pointed ears or whiskers.

wrong.A: A blue sky is not a cat pattern in the text.
wrong.C: A red ball is not mentioned.
wrong.D: Green grass is not mentioned.

MID.stem: The article says the computer "adjusts" its math. What does adjusts mean?
options: Hides completely
Changes a little
Counts out loud
Writes down
MID.why: After a wrong guess the computer changes its math a little and tries again.

wrong.A: The computer does not hide its math.
wrong.C: Counting out loud is not the meaning.
wrong.D: Writing down is not the meaning.

MID.stem: What makes a computer quite accurate in the end?
options: Many tries and small changes
One very long program
A person doing the work
A bigger and bigger screen
MID.why: The article says that after many tries, with small changes after each wrong guess, the computer becomes accurate.

wrong.B: The article says it learns from data, not one long program.
wrong.C: The computer is the one that adjusts its math.
wrong.D: Screens are not mentioned.

MID.stem: Why does the author begin with a phone that types your words and a map app?
options: To sell phones to readers
To teach how to use a map
To warn about traffic jams
To show AI in daily life
MID.why: These are everyday examples of machines that learned, which makes the topic feel real.

wrong.A: The article does not sell phones.
wrong.B: The article does not teach map use.
wrong.C: The traffic warning is only an example.

HIGH.stem: In what year was Saudi Arabia's national authority for data and AI established?
HIGH.why: The article says the authority was established in 2019.

wrong.A: The article says 2019, not 2009.
wrong.C: 2029 is in the future.
wrong.D: 1999 is too early.

HIGH.stem: The article says AI predicts which roads will become "congested." What does congested mean?
options: Crowded and slow
New and smooth
Closed and empty
Wet and slippery
HIGH.why: A map app warns about traffic, so congested roads are crowded.

wrong.B: Warnings about traffic do not mean new roads.
wrong.C: Empty roads would not need a warning.
wrong.D: Wet roads are not mentioned.

HIGH.stem: What problem leads engineers to use machine learning?
options: Computers are far too slow
Phones have very small screens
People forget all the data
Some tasks have too many rules
HIGH.why: The article says some tasks involve far too many rules to write, so engineers give the computer examples.

wrong.A: Speed is not the stated problem.
wrong.B: Screen size is not mentioned.
wrong.C: Forgetting data is not mentioned.

HIGH.stem: The article says AI does not truly understand the world. What does this suggest about a phone that types your words?
options: It must feel the way you feel
It can work without real thought
It will always type it perfectly
It has learned to think like us
HIGH.why: If AI lacks real understanding, the phone can still match speech to words without knowing what they mean.

wrong.A: The article says AI does not feel anything as people do.
wrong.C: The article says mistakes can happen and people must check.
wrong.D: The article says AI does not think exactly like a person.
